speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need both to work seamlessly together in what is, essentially, a very private and emotional affair – the birth of a family.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our dream is for every adopted child to have a good home and a family to take care of and to love them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I shall now make a few points about the Bill.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this case, I would like to ask if the threshold of "strong ties" is sufficiently high.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My question lies in the case of joint applications, which are allowed as long as both applicants are Permanent Residents (PRs).

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If the test is that of ties to one's country, should not one applicant, minimally, be a Singapore Citizen?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yes, PRs do have some degree of permanence, but they do move on when circumstances change.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, there are those who renounce it after the first term, or there could be others who have had their PRs, subsequently, not renewed or approved.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I agree with this as a matter of efficiency and also as a signal of how high we set the bar for qualifications.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, even as we have safeguards to disqualify applicants with certain prescribed offences, we do allow exceptions if the Court is satisfied that these individuals have reformed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have a related point, however, on how this relates to the wider point on the protection of children.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our duty of care towards the child must be of the same level when it comes to birth parents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As I had indicated earlier in my speech at this year's Committee of Supply debate on MSF's budget, we must be as prompt and forceful in separating a child from birth parents or families where they are deemed to be "harmful" to the child.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister say how this is provided for, if not in this Bill, then in other legislation relating to oversight and responses to child abuse and how parents who have committed serious offences are dealt with insofar as their ability to continue their parenting duties?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have, over the years, spoken quite a few times on the status of single parents and how our definition of "family" should expand to include these parents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a result of this provision for sole applicants, one question may arise for single parents who subsequently marry.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Specifically, what happens to a child if the sole parent goes on to legally marry someone of the same gender overseas?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This issue is one which opens itself up to strong debate, but I would say, as far as the issue of adoption is concerned, the "overriding consideration" that I spoke of at the start of the speech still holds – which is, the centrality of the child and for every adopted child to have a good home and a family to love them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If that condition holds, I would say there is much that the Bill can stay silent on and allow the circumstances of each specific case to be examined on its own merits, whether the single parent marries here or overseas and what the family unit, eventually, comprises.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I end with two specific points on regulating institutions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, how do we ensure or strengthen the assessment process for prospective adoptive parents?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can we ask for more testimonials and references to attest to the parents' character, as well as for specific performance indicators?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this case, I opine that more is better.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I agree with the placing of the onus, but I would like to add that we might want to impose annual affirmations and declarations on the part of applicants.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This reduces the chances of declarations being overlooked and removes an excuse of forgetfulness for applicants.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Again, in this case, it is better to be safe than sorry.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To some extent, this is a duty which extends to all persons who are vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is our collective duty to care for those who are unable to care for themselves and to put up rules, both for private conduct and in our institutions that work towards the flourishing of children within families.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Speaking from personal experience, what I have learnt is that the adopted child blesses and enriches the family.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My wish is that everyone listening to this speech today would seriously consider adoption, regardless of whether you have biological children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I must also take this time to commend MSF for the good work they have done so far, not only in tabling this Bill, but the hard work over the years in working with stakeholders, parents and children in striving towards creating more awareness and support for adoption and facilitating the process of adoption.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also wonderful voluntary welfare organisation (VWO) partners who do silent, selfless and courageous work in this space – such as Safe Place, Touch Community Services, aLife and so many more ground-up and committed organisations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Bill aims to find a good home for every child identified for adoption and I stand strongly in support of this.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In some cases, a baby's adoption status is treated as a secret.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, adoption can be celebrated as an act of love.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In that light, I support having disclosure briefings because it is best to disclose to the child as early as possible while helping the child understand that he or she is loved.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When our daughter was still young, my wife and I would tell her that she came from her "Tummy Mommy's" tummy, but she was born in our hearts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I understand that many would be concerned whether such disclosure would affect the child adversely.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I have thought about this and I believe we should tell the child about his or her adoption and do this as early as possible.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Inevitably, the child will realise that he or she is adopted and will wonder why it was kept a secret.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He or she will think that perhaps, there was something to be ashamed of.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A better approach, in my humble view, is for adoptive parents to explain adoption in a manner that is positive and affirming and showing the child that he or she belongs to a family and is loved equally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My wife and I have four children and all of them are treated and loved equally – no difference.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill also stands to break cycles of abuse and neglect and this is very important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With record numbers of child abuse cases in 2020 and 2021, we need to work harder to protect our young because they are vulnerable and cannot speak up or defend themselves.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With this Bill, more children will be able to be removed from abuse and neglect but, consequently, we will need more prospective parents willing to parent these children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The need to protect the best interests of the child means that certain behaviour that might compromise a child's welfare should be outlawed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the unavoidable fact is that commercial surrogacy invites a very high risk of exploiting the woman who rents her womb.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Surrogacy also invites so many middlemen and agents' fees.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many of these women who rent out their wombs come from developing countries and do so out of desperation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Surrogacy, in my view, should not be allowed in Singapore, or overseas for that matter, on account of the high possibility that women will be exploited.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of commercial surrogacy, adoption is a very real alternative.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We want to promote the ideal – which is not-for-profit adoption of Singaporean babies to Singaporean couples facilitated by non-commercial VWOs and MSF.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And, by "couples", I mean a husband and wife.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would also like to speak up in support of pregnant ladies who make the difficult and life-giving decision to keep their pregnancy and give their babies up for adoption.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this selfless manner, an unplanned pregnancy can create a wonderful family unit for the adoptive parents.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill arises out of a greater aim to create a greater space for adoption within our society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My sincere aspiration is that we, as a society, see adoption as equally attractive as having biological children and both can come hand-in-hand as routes to starting a family.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This positive framing of adoption can invite more prospective adoptive parents to come forward and put their names down and also for more unplanned pregnancies to lead to adoption instead of abortions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Then MSF can match the two lists together and facilitate more adoptions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having a child, whether adopted or biological, is not always easy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It will not always be smooth, but love solves all things.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope that there will be many more adoptions in Singapore in the decades to come.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To prospective adoptive parents, do take the leap of faith and walk the journey.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is a wonderful team in MSF and I admire them and am thankful to them for all their hard work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I stand here in Parliament strongly advocating for the incredibly worthy cause of adoption.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And for this reason, I support this timely Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.10 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.50 pm until 5.10 pm.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I am pleased by the added rigour, scrutiny and support that will be soon embedded in the screening, selection and post-adoption processes, to ultimately, safeguard the well-being and the rights of children across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Please allow me to share a few thoughts on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: One, on the requirement for adopters to undergo suitability assessments; two, on breaking cycles of abuse and neglect; and three, on the suitability and criteria to adopt.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This is to ensure a robust due diligence process which ascertains the fitness, readiness and suitability of adoption applicants.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be a comprehensive evaluation of the child's medical, mental and emotional status?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, will full disclosure of these details be shared with potential adoptive parents?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, the mental health and condition of adopted children are a concern and potential adopters should be made aware of the unique needs of the child they are adopting.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I move to my next point on breaking cycles of abuse and neglect.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I fully agree that access to a safe, stable environment is paramount to the health, happiness and development of the child.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Second, like overcomers, birth parents may be deemed unfit or unwilling to care for children at a point of time.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: But what if they can overcome and be deemed able and willing to parent later?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In these instances, would there be an opportunity for the birth parents to reconcile with their birth children?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, on the criteria for suitability to adopt, my hope is for us to be a progressive nation and begin to have conversations on non-traditional family units.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Although I respect the policies in place today, it is my hope that, in time, we dispense with evaluations of suitability based on sexual orientation or relationship status when the key qualifications and thresholds for suitability have been satisfied.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition, Singapore's birth and fertility rate has been declining.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And adoption is one of the top options for couples who aspire to parenthood.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Adoption is, thus a matter of interest to our society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: An adoption order granted by the Court is, in effect, a termination of the legal relationship between a child and his/her biological parents, and adoption means transferring all rights and responsibilities in caring for the child to the adoptive parents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I wish to touch on matters relating to three key stakeholder groups: the children to be adopted, the adoptive parents and the adoption agencies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I fully agree with the Ministry's undergirding principle behind this suite of amendments in the Bill – that the top priority is to guard the welfare of the child.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of the stakeholders involved in the adoption process are adults: prospective adopters, biological parents, adoption agency operators.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But the person that is most impacted remains to be the child who is up for adoption.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My question to the Minister is, therefore, how the voice of the child can be better sought and heard.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: All the names I use hereon are not the real names of the persons involved, but all of them are people I know.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the case of one of my young teenaged residents, I call him "Weng", the stress and uncertainty he endured during the adoption process was very hard for him.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Weng's biological father, in a foreign country, had abused both him and his mother.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: His mother remarried a Singaporean who discovered the option of adoption only after quite a long period of appeals to agencies and through me, the Member of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Throughout the period of adoption, Weng, the young man, expressed great fear and anxiety of being rejected in this adoption application and being sent back to his home country.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Weng really wanted to reside in Singapore with his mother and stepfather and wants to serve National Service when it is time.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am so glad he is one now.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Another young resident, "QH", had to return to China to fend for himself at age 21, whilst his biological mother remained in Singapore with his biological half-brother and Singaporean stepfather.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I supported part of his education, because fees were very high for him as a foreigner here and I often wished he could have become one of Singapore's sons.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One of my former students, "Boon", is a Singaporean child with special needs who was fostered as a toddler, because he was abandoned, until he was 21, through the Ministry's arrangement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Could Boon have been put up for adoption earlier?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He was fostered for more than a decade.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How long, therefore, would it take under the Bill, the new Act, if approved, to propose and facilitate the adoption of fostered children like Boon who were abandoned from young?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on the voice of the adoptive parents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the process of preparing this speech, I spoke to a number of adoptive parents who have walked the journey.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are usually two main areas of concern: one, the long administrative process; and second, the unevenness of available information for them to make informed decisions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: That was step seven of, I think, 15 steps in MSF's portal, when I did a search.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Mothers, like Yen, ask if the new process would further lengthen the anxiety of bona fide prospective adopters.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How do the steps in the new process vary, in terms of the number of steps, quantity, duration and complexity?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How can the process be made more efficient whilst ensuring the welfare of the child remains a priority?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst essential steps to assess and prepare prospective adopters are made mandatory, which I fully support, are there other steps that can be consolidated or simplified and the flow of information across agencies be better shared?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second concern of adoptive parents is that of the uneven level of awareness amongst them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the words of one parent who spoke to me, "for us, the official road sort of 'ended' after MSF officially gave us the certification to become adoptive parents." Another one told me, "After the Home Study Report was done, we did not know where to go to look for the babies." They depended on the luck of the draw, to land the right lawyer to help them, the right social worker and the right adoption agency.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Several adoptive parents cited their search of agencies to be daunting and quoted some agencies to be "dubious" and "dodgy".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Surely, much more could be done to facilitate access to the needed information to help potential adoptive parents make better informed decisions and to cut short the process.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How can the better ones, that Mr Deputy Speaker spoke about just now, be recognised and engaged?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For the sustainability of the good players in the market, whether for profit or not, financial viability is necessary.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, can there be some way to help them?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I seek the Ministry's considered responses to the concerns I have raised for the child, adoptive parents and adoptive agencies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I note that the Bill contains certain provisions of the Adoption of Children Act 1939 while also codifying certain other current practices, and I would like to seek clarifications on just certain parts of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: ASA is required to be issued by an authorised adoption agency pursuant to the requirements of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Clause 14 further provides that a valid ASA is one that is issued in the form specified by and contains all the necessary information required by GIA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Currently, only limited categories of prospective adoptive parents are required to obtain a favourable Home Study Report (HSR) before they are allowed to adopt, for example, for overseas adoptive children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The HSR assessment is usually carried out by one of the four Social Service Agencies (SSAs) specifically authorised by MSF to provide certain adoption services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One such organisation, Touch Community Services, has provided a helpful explanation on the purpose of HSR on their website.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They explained that HSR is to assess a person's suitability and readiness to adopt a child.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The assessment is required before the adoptive parents start searching for a suitable child or before initiating legal adoption proceedings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The home study process involves interviews, screenings, home visits and applicants will be assessed on areas, such as their motivation to adopt, views on adoption, family, marital, medical and employment history, childcare arrangement, parenting styles and other relevant information, involving adoption and adoptive parenting.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And if ASA will not replace HSR, how would ASA add value to the current HSR regime beyond the ASA being a formal certification by the adoption agency that these applicants are suitable to be adoptive parents?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For any other group of applicants not currently subject to the HSR procedure, for example, a step-parent adopting a child of his or spouse from a previous marriage, may I know what is the expected rigour of the ASA assessment expected, for example, when compared to the current HSR process?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How will GIA ensure that all ASAs comply with the requirements and standards expected under the Bill or any subsidiary legislation?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am also curious why the Government did not consider it fit to allow the current four SSAs, which are issuing HSRs to issue ASAs, instead of getting the authorised adoption agencies to do so.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Since the four SSAs are already issuing HSRs, it would seem reasonable and consistent for them to do the ASA assessment and issue the ASAs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am also concerned about the additional cost to adoption which may arise from the requirement of ASA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The expenses for the adoption of overseas children are already quite significant and it is not easily affordable to some.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Clause 10 of the Bill allows the Minister to designate or authorise adoption agencies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I agree with the Bill setting guidelines for permissible adoption-related payments, requiring all our adoption agencies to publish information on their fees, as well as other provisions, criminalising undesirable behaviour.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is important to ensure that agencies uphold acceptable standards and moral practices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, I am concerned about the possible compliance costs which may be incurred by such authorised adoption agencies and whether such costs will be passed on to the adoptive parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am concerned that the requirement should not lead to an increase in the cost of adoption fees and expenses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I can understand some of these difficult cases, the concerns about their birth parents being continually unfit to take care of their children, or even be abusive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I can also understand that some of these children may even have good and close relationships with their foster parents, making adoption a worthwhile consideration.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Nevertheless, people may change for the better over time and live to regret their past actions, while legal adoption, unlike fostering, adds a permanent and irreversible seal to an end to the legal relationship between birth parents and their children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Rehabilitation efforts, may, for some, involve a longer time than others.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How do we decide between continuing a child under foster care or putting the child in foster care up for adoption?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, I understand that adopted children, who were foreigners at the time of birth are given citizenship at the time of the formalisation of adoption.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, ICA requires such children to take the oath of renunciation, allegiance and loyalty when they reach 21, pursuant to Article 124(1) of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are no other options for these children, unlike other categories, such as children who keep dual nationalities from birth, either by the parents' choice or at least one of the adoptive parents has a foreign nationality.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Currently, MSF states on its website that prospective adopters are strongly encouraged to attend a disclosure workshop on talking with one's adopted child about adoption.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The workshop will help one to understand why adopted children should know about their status and how adoptive parents can approach the subject.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These briefings have been a part of the adoption procedure for some time now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There is quite a lot of literature on the benefits of disclosure, particularly early disclosure of the fact of adoption to the adopted child.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the days of old, many parents would not tell their adopted children the fact of their adoption and some would find out later on in their life, through different sources or by accident.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many adopted children do not react well to discovering this later in their life.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some time ago, a father shared with me his painful experience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He and his wife had adopted a child from a neighbouring country some years ago and did not disclose the fact of adoption to the child.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As the child developed a different complexion from his adoptive parents as he got older, he was teased about it and had a tough time in school.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One day, he confronted his parents about it and his parents admitted to him that he was adopted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, he struggled to accept this revelation in his mid-teens and why he was not told about it earlier.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He developed difficult behavioural issues right through his early adulthood.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Though not mandatory, my wife and I agreed at the onset that we should disclose to our child that she is adopted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We started by sharing with her stories of adoption even when she was a baby.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In recent years, we started telling her that we are her adoptive parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: She knows that she has a "Tummy Mommy" and a "Forever Mommy".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is still a work in progress in our disclosure journey.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We expect that, in future years, we would have more and deeper conversations with her about her adoption, but we are glad that we have started this journey of disclosure some time ago.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I understand that there may still be parents who may not be comfortable with disclosure and I sincerely hope that, by my sharing, I can also encourage some of those who may still have doubts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am in a support group of adoptive families that was initially set up by the SSA which helped us with our home study report the Lutheran Community Care Services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Pre-COVID-19, the group's parents and children had met from time to time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the group will be meeting up again soon with the relaxation of safe management measure (SMM) conditions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My daughter also meets up with other friends who are adopted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Recently, a staff worker from the Lutheran Community Care Services sent to our support group a video on disclosure which I found to be very encouraging and thought-provoking.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that adoptive parents and all stakeholders can continue to work together to encourage more parents about the benefits of disclosure and also to help adoptive parents and children along both their disclosure journey and, indeed, their adoption journey.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For many would-be parents, the little pink "+" sign on the home pregnancy test kit is a moment of incredible joy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For other couples, this journey may be prolonged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As this House discussed last month, higher ages for marriage have been accompanied by greater challenges for childbearing, although, with the intervention of modern science, many are able to conceive and birth children of their own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are yet others for whom this route is closed, who find themselves unable to have biological children of their own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And, of course, there are those who see the provision of a home to a child, for whom this would otherwise not be available, as a noble calling in and of itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For such latter groups of households, desirous of having the pitter-patter of tiny feet as any other, there is one other route – becoming the parent of a child who has been born in otherwise undesirable circumstances, which led to the child being given up for adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As any "forever" parent would tell you, there is absolutely no difference, insofar as becoming a father or mother is concerned, when one holds that baby, boy or girl, in one's hands for the very first time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Adoption is the way that these parents have been able to experience that joy of parenthood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many of the proposed amendments and refinements are both necessary and very much welcomed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, I have concerns about how some of these measures may, inadvertently, introduce unintended consequences that run counter to the child's interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They have to do with pre-adoption procedures, post-adoption recognition, both for parents and the child, counselling for adoptive parents and the regulation of adoption agents, all of which I plan to elaborate on in my speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clause 13, which formally requires participation in a briefing on the disclosure of the child's adoption status, formalises the existing practice of strongly encouraging attendance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is fully in line with both evidence that points to the psychological benefits as well as the ethical responsibility of doing so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, reconciling the need to perform a home study for not just foreign, but also Singaporean children, is consistent with the fact that home dynamics and the suitability of parents to adopt does not discriminate by national origin.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All potential parents should be carefully assessed while simultaneously being transparently confronted with concerns that would trigger a rejection and, thereby, be allowed to proactively address any red flags that serve as a barrier to adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While some prospective parents may find the assessment process intrusive and unfair, it is important to remember that pre-emptively ruling out couples who are unsuitable for parenthood is, ultimately, in the best interests of the child.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The last thing we would wish for an adopted child is the need to face the trauma of yet another parental rejection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Pre-COVID-19, the process would, generally, be done and dusted in about nine months.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I, myself, find this duration somewhat poignant – and practice reflected this reality with the initial Dependant's Pass issued for a nine-month period, with little need for extension in most cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This may well have been reflective of the fact that the pandemic introduced inevitable delays into the process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unsurprisingly, foreign adoptions effectively ceased in the earlier phases of COVID-19.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, even as we return to normal, there has not been any reversion to the practice of the original nine-month duration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, one must understand the mindset by which humans, such as you and I, operate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With additional time, the sense of urgency to complete the task often diminishes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: How many of us have drafted our Parliamentary speeches well in advance of the deadline?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And it risks dragging out the uncertainty faced by adoptive parents; imagine not knowing for certain that, after a full one-and-a-half years of caring for a child, they would not, for sure, be taken away.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A 21-month timeframe for completion also throws a wrench into the prospective parents who may wish to adopt more than one child, since they are unlikely to initiate the adoption of a second until the first is complete.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I also believe that there are reasonable adjustments to the current procedures that can expedite the process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the moment, there are four accredited SSAs that have been tasked by MSF to perform HSR.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The report itself is exhaustive and intrusive, and understandably so, since it is critical to ensure the suitability of a couple to raise an adopted child.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But what is somewhat puzzling is how a very similar set of questions is posed by MSF itself, despite the fact that they have access to HSR and that HSR is produced by agencies accredited by MSF itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, while interviews by MSF following HSR are justifiable – these occur after the arrival of the child, which does alter family dynamics – the replication of the report seems to me to be less so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would submit that the resources dedicated to repeating HSR are much better dedicated towards ensuring the integrity of the process, followed by the accrediting agencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, before the in-principle approval (IPA), which kickstarts the entire adoption process, is issued, MSF would, typically, interview the birth parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is, of course, important and necessary to respect the rights of the biological parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this step can be concluded and closed once IPA has been issued.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, why would it make sense to reopen psychological scars, encourage rumination and prevarication and risk imparting a sense of doubt and regret thereafter?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What would it mean for the hitherto adoptive parents if, after a year and a half down the road, the birth mother somehow changes her mind?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, such parents face the same emotions of loss should the child be suddenly taken away from them and of fear of deep commitment to the child before the adoption is finalised, should the adoption process somehow fail.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What this would mean for the child is a home environment characterised by uncertainty and this is the last thing you would want to wish for a child who is already facing unprecedented volatility in their family life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is why clauses 46 and 47 spell out, in no uncertain terms, the status of the adoptive parents vis-à-vis the child after the adoption order is issued.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, certain rights pertaining to parents do not appear to be well-handled by the related and consequential amendments spelt out in part 9.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, clause 77 amends the definition of a Dependant's Pass in the Child Development Co-Savings Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, as far as I am aware, parents are unable to purchase health insurance for the child or to add them to a family health insurance package before formal adoption is complete.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus, while they remain on the Dependant's Pass, parents are unable to have the financial assurance that one will be able to take one's son or daughter to the doctor, especially in the early months when all manner of health issues may unexpectedly present themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It strikes me that some exemption should be afforded to those on a Dependant's Pass to be added to insurance in this case since the child's health does not respect the timelines dictated by the adoption process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if MOM cannot process a concessionary rate until after the child has definitively received their citizenship, a rebate for prior months after the change of status may, in fact, be warranted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a final example, consider the 12-week paid adoption leave granted by MOM.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is unclear to me why the three-month bonding and care period should exclude the father.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As this House debated last month, it makes much more sense to have a longer period of shared parental leave which either parent can draw on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is all the more so, given how the adoptive mother will not have to undergo the typical postpartum physiological and psychological recovery process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will this timeline be altered by the current practice where Dependant's Passes are issued for 21 months?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clauses 35 and 45 now afford the Court the right to order mediation and counselling for parents, so long as it is beneficial to the well-being of the child.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The former clause comes into play during the adoption process or the latter applies post-adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is difficult to quibble about requiring such intervention before adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, there remains limited clarity about the adoptive parents' relationship status and background which could influence the success of the adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, to extend the power to do so after the conclusion of adoption proceedings indefinitely strikes me as an open invitation for the state to exercise its power to excessively intervene in family dynamics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I understand that conflicts at any time after the child is adopted is possible, that open-ended nature of the clause may, potentially, discriminate between adoptive and non-adoptive families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would it not be better to introduce a time-delimited requirement within the context of this particular Bill and to rely on existing laws governing child protection to stipulate mandatory counselling?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Parts 6 and 7, notably, clauses 54(4) and 60(3), spell out punishments in the form of monetary fines for adoption agents that fail to comply with the requirements stated in the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the Bill appears to fall short of taking the next step of holding frequent or flagrant violators to more permanent account.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, MSF, currently, declines to mete out any durable punishments, falling back on the argument that parents working with ACRA-registered adoption agents are engaged in private arrangements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It remains unclear whether this means MSF will permanently bar an individual or agency from the industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These need not mean that each agent must be accredited per se, but there is, at least, a record of the most systematic violators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Children are not commodities to be traded and providers that adopt – pardon the pun – poor practices should not be allowed to continue to do so repeatedly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government fully understands the benefits of regulatory discipline associated with official registries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I see little reason why this should not apply with equal force to adoption agents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have raised a number of concerns – many practical in nature – that I hope the Ministry will take into consideration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the Bill, as a whole, encapsulates many improvements that will help create more happy families in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And for this reason, it has my clear and unequivocal support.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a beacon of hope for couples who are unable to conceive, but desire to have children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My speech will focus on four aspects of the Bill: one, giving priority to prospective adopters who have strong ties to Singapore; two, safeguards to prevent persons convicted of serious crimes from adopting; three, suitability assessment for all prospective adopters; and four, post-adoption support for adoptive families.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my Meet-the-People Sessions, I came across several residents who are either adopting or have adopted the children of their foreign spouses.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After the adoption process is completed, these adoptive step-parents have expressed concerns and difficulties in affording the educational fees of their step-children, who are often foreign students.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many appeal for permanent residence and citizenship status for their adopted stepchildren to try to reduce their school fees in Singapore, but this process takes time.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope to seek clarification from MSF on what may be the safeguards in place to ensure that Singaporeans under such circumstances are given full counsel on the full financial implications of bringing their stepchildren up in Singapore to ensure that the welfare of the adopted children are taken care of.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A good adoptive relationship depends on the good character of the adoptive parents to instil good behaviours and set good examples for their adoptive children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, I would like to understand how MSF intends to determine the nature of offences to be prescribed in the legislation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will serious crimes be determined by the category of crimes, length of imprisonment and/or the amount of fine imposed?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my view, even for those with non-serious offences, as it will be difficult to guarantee that there will be no risk of re-offending, it may be in the best interests of children being put up for adoption to also be protected.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is especially if the criteria for serious or non-serious crimes are not easy to prescribe.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there are no means-testing schemes to ensure that the fee would remain affordable for prospective adopters.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Several established research studies have consistently shown the long-term effects that adopted children faced, which often persist into adulthood.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The research showed that adopted children are at higher risk of developing behavioural and emotional issues, such as anxiety, depression and delinquent behaviour.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would agree with the majority of the respondents during the public consultation process that the support services not be made mandatory, but are provided on a needs basis, when it is required.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, I welcome the Adoption of Children Bill tabled by MSF.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The adoption of a child is very meaningful.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is because it enables children who need a family, especially those under state care, to find a home suitable for them.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It also gives couples who cannot have children of their own a glimmer of hope and helps them form a happy family.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, the Bill proposes that, for joint applicants, at least one parent must be a citizen, or both must be PRs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At my weekly Meet-the-People sessions, I came across residents who adopted a foreign stepson or stepdaughter because they have married a foreign spouse.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, as they could not afford to pay for the tuition fees of foreign students, they hope to apply for PR status for their stepchildren to lighten the burden of school fees.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I hope that MSF will consider certain measures to help these applicants.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, the Bill proposes that persons who have committed serious offences would not be allowed to adopt children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that MSF will clarify what constitutes a serious offence.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While limiting the eligibility of ex-convicts who have committed serious crimes to adopt children to protect the safety and welfare of children, we cannot prevent ex-convicts who have committed non-serious crimes from re-offending, thus affecting the development of the adopted children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I hope that MSF will consider giving lower priority to ex-offenders who have committed non-serious crimes, to better protect the safety of the adopted children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, the Bill proposes to give the Court the power to order adoptive families to attend counselling, if necessary.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many studies have shown that adopted children are at a higher risk of developing emotional problems than those who grow up in their biological families.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I hope that MSF will continue to provide social services for adopted children until they reach the age of 21, so that we can detect and treat potential mental illnesses early.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, there are many wonderful stories of adopted children finding good homes, where they are unreservedly loved by their adoptive parents.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For adoptive parents, it can also be a rewarding journey of parenthood, so that their adopted children can get a better life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A safe and happy childhood leads to lifelong and intergenerational benefits for health, productivity and mental wellness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This stems from my personal experience being a father of five kids.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The sad reality is that not all families are equipped or able to care for their children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is notwithstanding how much they want to.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These situations may be present at the time of birth or come into being during their childhood years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Personally, I believe the overriding principle for adoption is to provide them with psychological safety, as well as the caring and supportive environment that they need.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have a few clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, will all the changes to child adoption laws apply to foreign adoptees, where the adopting family is based in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I support the decision to prevent persons convicted of serious crimes from adopting.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That said, I also believe in second chances.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I trust the effectiveness of our prison rehabilitation programmes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thus, I believe that the current position is the right balance between caution and giving second chances.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, how does the Ministry determine whether the person has been adequately reformed, to be capable of providing care to a vulnerable child?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will this restriction, based on the conviction of serious crimes, also apply to the immediate family members of the adopting couple?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These would be people who also live with or spend significant amounts of time in the company of the adopted child.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If the applicant or said family members have committed serious crimes abroad, will they also be subjected to the same restrictions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the amendment that seeks to provide more clarity on circumstances, where consent from the birth parents can be dispensed with, if it is in the child's welfare.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, there may sometimes be compatibility issues between the adopting family and the adopted child.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What intervention and support measures will the Ministry provide to the family and their adopted child, if these issues occur?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Quite often, this may happen when the parents adopt a special needs child or one with some behavioural baggage, but underestimate the effort and resources required to bring him or her up.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I know of a couple who adopted a child with special needs from the Philippines.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Caring for the child is not easy and I applaud the couple's efforts in providing a safe and loving home for him.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Other than briefing the potential parents with regard to the potential needs of the child, will the Ministry consider providing greater support to parents willing to care for such children?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to, hopefully, prevent the need for the Court to make an order against the adopting parents for the child's welfare.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill stipulates for prospective adoptive parents to attend a compulsory pre-adoption briefing, where they learn more about the adoption process and related issues, before they can apply to adopt.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Should there be a more extensive preparation course and follow up?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there mandatory health check-ups and mental health assessments for the adoptees, before an adoption procedure is finalised?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, what if the adopted child is unable to get along with the rest of the siblings and other family members?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry encourage adoptive parents and their families, where practical, to participate in respite fostering activities, if they seem unsure about adoption?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this way, the family can gauge whether they really have what it takes to welcome someone new into their families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This should not be a test, but it could be an avenue for families to determine their readiness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I would suggest that part of the adoption process should include training or conversations with adopting parents and their families, to aid them with such decisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The discussions should cover the sibling relationship issues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this way, these conversations can be a whole family affair.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Deputy Speaker, does the Ministry intend to actively raise awareness and encourage adoption of children who have been under state care?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does this figure compare with the number of children who are under state care?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is the percentage of those in state care who have been identified for adoption?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the criteria for these children to be deemed suitable for adoption?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I support the amendments to ensure that adoption agencies publish their fees in a transparent manner and only charge the permitted payments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While advertising adoptees with identifying information is understandably prohibited, perhaps a generic awareness campaign on local child adoption could help to shed more light on the values and realities of child adoption.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the new laws, I believe that Singapore will be a safer place for vulnerable children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore will also benefit from a new generation of children who would have otherwise fallen by the wayside.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In my maiden speech in this Parliament during the Debate on the President's Address one and a half years ago, I spoke about how we can be richer as a nation, if we help one another.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are just emerging from the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But there is other help that is needed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need the community to come together and to care for those who may be less fortunate and may be in need of a loving home and loving relationships.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is great value for us to do more for one another.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Natural families already have many obstacles to overcome, to achieve stability and provide a safe and comfortable environment for children to thrive and grow.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I imagine that adoptive parents would face even more challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Dedicating resources, energy and giving of your lives to a child outside of your natural family is, undoubtedly, one of the most selfless acts of humanity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While this number is not large, each and every adoption could mean a better future for the child, especially if the birth parents are unable or unsuited to raise the child properly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I, therefore, support the extensive proposals to enhance our local adoption laws and practices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, the issue of the Courts dispensing with the consent of birth parents in the adoption process is not new, as there are prevailing case law examples.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would also like to ask what will be the protections given to the adopted child and the adoptive family, to prevent birth parents who did not provide their consent, from harassing the family?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In cases where the birth parent was found to have intentionally caused grievous physical hurt or mental trauma to the child, it is vital that we do all we can to help the child get a clean break from the cycle of abuse.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Adoptive parents, too, should be protected from harassment and be given a safe and conducive environment to care for their adopted child.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Next, I will touch on deterring undesirable behaviours in the adoption sector.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Specifically, the Bill proposes to make adoption practices more transparent by making clear what are allowable adoption-related payments and to require all adoption agencies to clearly publish information on their fees.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But is this sufficient to combat existing unscrupulous practices in the adoption sector?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A recent news report published by CNA, followed the story of an adoptive parent who tried to adopt a newborn in Singapore four years ago, but was forced to return the baby to the birth parent after refusing to pay questionable additional fees to the birth parent and the adoption agency.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Is this a prevalent practice in Singapore, where adoptive children are being, and I quote, "sold as merchandise" to the highest bidder?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How many such cases have MSF come across in the past five years?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can MSF, therefore, consider regulating the fees charged by adoption agencies in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While I understand that adoption agencies currently charge different rates due to a variety of reasons, such as childbirth expenses, we should rein in adoption agencies that try to profiteer from adoptive parents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Simply put, we can, and must, end the abhorrent practice of giving babies to the highest bidder.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, I hope that more Singaporeans can consider becoming foster parents to vulnerable children and young persons who are in need of a loving home environment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can MSF provide an update on its efforts to encourage more families to step forward to become foster parents?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Various research papers and anecdotal stories posted online have documented the multitude of challenges involved in fostering.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It can, indeed, be stressful to be foster parents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In addition to the traditional stressors of caregiving, foster parents must build rapport with the child, who often might come from a troubled background and, therefore, finds it difficult to trust his new caregivers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some foster parents have shared that they sometimes received a late call-up to foster a child, and this would spark a last-minute shopping rush for clothes and essential items and to make urgent childcare arrangements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To alleviate these challenges, can the Ministry consider providing foster parents with additional childcare leave, beyond what are already provided for under the Child Development Co-Savings Act and the Employment Act?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we enhance the Act to improve the adoption processes and weed out undesirable behaviour within the industry, I also hope that more Singaporeans will consider fostering and adopting children who are in need of a loving family.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For those aged between seven and 12, Government-paid extended childcare leave is only two days.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: After all, toddlers and preschoolers need as much, if not more, time than infants to bond with their adoptive mothers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The first few months of the adoption are a major and critical adjustment period for both mother and child.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With 12 weeks of adoption leave, the mother will be better enabled to understand the traits and needs of her adopted child.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The child will also benefit immensely from the dedicated attention of his or her adoptive mother in a new home and, in some cases, a new country.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Increasing the adoption leave for mothers of toddlers and preschoolers will also encourage more suitable local couples to consider adopting children in state care who are typically older.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As the Bill proposes to clarify the threshold for the dispensation of consent for the welfare of children under state care, such a provision will be helpful in meeting the future rising needs of older children being adopted into stable families.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My second suggestion is to provide funding for adoptive parents' support groups.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Funding would be helpful for authorised adoption agencies to facilitate more regular support group sessions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through such sessions, social workers will be able to detect problems faced by adoptive families and assist them in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Parents can also turn to these groups for emotional support and useful advice at different stages of their children's growth and development.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Unique issues that they may face would include disclosure, family conflict between the adopted and biological children or other family members, or a budding romance between adopted children or between an adopted child and a biological child, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I see the importance of support groups and strongly encourage adoptive families to participate.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   My third suggestion is regarding the school fees paid by non-citizen stepchildren in the process of being adopted.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Until they are adopted and become Singapore Citizens, they have to pay international student fees, which are much higher than those that are paid by Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents (PRs).

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These fees would impose a heavy burden on most families.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of these children may even have to miss school until they are adopted and become citizens.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For more complex cases, the adoption process may take up to two years.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This break in their learning is a disservice to growing children.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have received some feedback from a number of Singaporean men who are married to divorcees from China with children from their previous marriages.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many of these men would like to adopt their stepchildren.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the Chinese embassy requires that the biological fathers have to endorse and sign the adoption papers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In some cases, there are delays in the ex-spouses' negotiation of terms and conditions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In other cases, the biological Chinese fathers may refuse to sign.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the interests of the children at heart, I would like to request the Government to consider charging these children school fees that are similar to those paid by PRs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government may impose certain conditions, such as indications of these foreigner children setting their roots here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is not clear to me if post-adoption reviews will be required or how it will be implemented for adoptions here.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Bill proposes to empower the Court to order attendance of relevant support services, such as counselling and mediation, if required at any point during the adoption proceedings or after an order has been made.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, this is different from a routinely scheduled post-adoption assessment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For children adopted from China, the China Centre for Children's Welfare and Adoption (CCCWA) requires post-placement reports.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These reports are to be prepared by accredited agencies here and submitted to CCCWA.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For stepchildren and kinship adoptions, the adoptive parents are required to undergo at least one post-adoption assessment within three years from the adoption registration in China.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For children adopted from the social welfare institution, parents need to complete six post placement reports at the sixth month, first year, second year, third year, fourth year and fifth year milestones.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At first glance, the Bill affects a small number of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, for the new parents who choose to adopt, for the children who are adopted and for the biological parents of the children put up for adoption, the laws and processes of adoption have an immense impact to them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, I am heartened that MSF is proposing a set of comprehensive and timely amendments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Notwithstanding my support for many parts of the Bill, I would like MSF to also clarify, particularly on the provision that allows for the judicial Courts to dispense with the consent of a relevant person, who is usually a biological parent, to a child being put up for adoption if certain thresholds are met.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: After all, if parents or guardians are deemed by the Courts to be extremely ill-suited to discharge their duties, then, surely, there must be a legal process where society can protect the child, by giving the child the opportunity to live outside bad, or even dangerous, influences of his or her biological parents or guardians.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, I do hope that MSF can provide the public clarity on the Government's considerations, as well as the steps that Government agencies will take, before the commencement of the Court process.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Will our social workers inform the biological parents or guardians at the earliest possible time if the social workers deem them to be heading down a path where the state takes their children away from them?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If so, how will the social workers inform these biological parents or guardians?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am fully aware that there are circumstances, such as serious abuse and neglect, where the state has to refer cases to the Courts immediately and at the first occurrence of such abuses.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But there are also circumstances that are less clear.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As fellow parliamentarians here, we all have our encounters with families that are embroiled in serious family disputes, violence, potential or actual abuses.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There are also parents that we see who are struggling with children with uncontrollable behaviours.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: What I worry about is that if the public is unclear about how this provision will be implemented, then some parents in families that require deep intervention from our social workers may withdraw from cooperating with MSF, out of a misplaced fear that their children will be taken away from them without their consent.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must also consider the issue on the other side.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There are also parents who are engaging in self-destructive behaviours or lifestyles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These parents may not be well-informed about the laws, such as ACA.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: By informing them of the consequences of their actions early on, it is possible that the fear of losing their children will inspire them to take a different path.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As such, I hope MSF can provide some clarity on this matter, even though I acknowledge it is not an easy balance to strike.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And will some children currently being fostered also have a chance to be adopted, and will the fostered parents be informed or consulted?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a step towards helping children identified for adoption find good homes, breaking cycles of abuse and neglect, and deterring undesirable behaviours in the adoption sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that the amendments proposed in this Bill contain suggestions surfaced in those consultations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the pre-adoption application requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the requirements that must be satisfied by applicants to obtain a favourable ASA?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister further clarify what are the requirements for the simpler ASA for adoption of a related child?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 22(1), during the relevant period, applicants for an ASA must notify the authorised adoption agency of any material change as soon as practicable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The relevant period starts on the day of an ASA application and ends the day after an adoption application has been made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With the child's welfare as the primary guiding principle in mind, can MSF share how it ensures the continued suitability of applicants after the adoption application has concluded?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, will MSF be releasing guidelines on the administrative requirements, legal processes and the relevant costs involved in the pre-adoption application to provide applicants with more guidance?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do understand there are diverse views on this issue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how MSF decided on the threshold for the dispensation of consent and also further details on when MSF will consider the dispensation of consent appropriate?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is about deterring undesirable behaviours in the adoption sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To safeguard the integrity of the adoption process, there should be sufficient mechanisms in place to sanction and deter undesirable behaviours that compromise a child's welfare.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, transparency in the amounts paid to adoption agencies will go some way in deterring undesirable behaviours through public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what mechanisms will be in place to enforce the publication of amounts to be paid to or through adoption agencies?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the penalties for adoption agencies that fail to publish such information?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also understand there are, currently, less than 10 private adoption agencies offering different suites of services at varying costs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister consider implementing a mandatory accreditation for all adoption agencies to standardise the practice and determine their suitability to operate?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A registry of accredited agencies could be published to recognise those that are committed towards the protection of children under their care.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may give prospective adopters better peace of mind as they embark on the journey towards parenthood.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For this report, they have to submit information pertaining to their reasons for adopting, their family, education, employment and health, among others.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the couples need to submit more detailed information with the new Bill?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The reason is that, generally, although not for all cases, adoptive couples tend to be older couples.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But, if the child to be adopted is 10 years old, this would mean that the couple may be up to 60 years old.
